prize_parts.citation: for a body of poetry, essay and hybrid narrative that remakes the boundaries between lyric, scholarship and visual form in dialogue with antiquity, joining formal daring to elegiac force

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Anne Carson, one prize part, one credited name. I did, however, test it against the chair's questions and the round-1 exchange, and my margin over Cărtărescu is narrower than it was. The case rests on what I can assess most directly: voice, formal and linguistic achievement, and sustained intellectual depth. Carson's voice is recognisable at the level of the line, and the achievement is one of language and form, not only of subject. Autobiography of Red turns a myth into a verse novel that holds erudition, desire and comedy together. Nox turns elegy into a material object. The chair asks which works beyond those two carry a durable core. From general public knowledge I would point to the essay Eros the Bittersweet, the lyric and mixed-form collections such as Plainwater, Men in the Off Hours and Decreation, and the book-length poem The Beauty of the Husband. Taken together they suggest that the recurring concerns are desire, loss, the pull of the ancient text and the fragment as a unit of thought. Those concerns return in changing forms over several decades, which I read as a method and not a string of one-off experiments. I would build the citation on the original poetry, essays and hybrid narrative, and leave translations and adaptations of Greek texts out as a ground. I accept that the question of whether scale or compact range weighs more is now what separates B045 from B004, and I resolve it on the criterion of sustained quality. I do not count scale as depth, and variety held together by a coherent core can show sustained quality. English is also a language in which committee members can read the sentences directly. Translation therefore distorts the evidence less for Carson than for Romanian or Chinese prose. That is an evidential advantage and not a literary one, so I give it limited weight. I have not read the full corpus and have not independently verified any text.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and I cannot dismiss it. A compact, formally varied corpus is harder to judge for uniform depth than a large novelistic oeuvre such as Cărtărescu's. Some of the effects depend on classical apparatus, book design and material format, which may not survive other editions or translation. Float, which is issued as a case of separate pamphlets, and parts of Nox are the clearest cases. Some later pieces appear occasional or performative, and part of the corpus is translation or adaptation. That makes a whole-oeuvre citation harder to draw than for a body of purely original work. Carlberg's question about significance beyond English-language and academic readerships is the one I find hardest to answer. My reply, the emotional directness of Nox and of the lyrics, remains a judgment and not an established fact. If readers who know the later volumes find the hybrid forms to be a narrowly appealing erudite mode, the case is considerably weaker than I now estimate.

responses.point: Mattson moved Carson up from fifth to a stronger alternative after Carlberg's argument for a citation covering the whole hybrid oeuvre. She still holds that Carson's achievement is harder to bound than Cărtărescu's sustained project of large-scale prose with a poetic root.
responses.response: I think your remaining objection is the right one: a bounded project is easier to credit than a varied one. I would answer that the boundary is the recurring core and the original forms, and not the genre label. I also share your caution that I cannot judge the design and Greek-apparatus effects from the text alone, so the citation should not rest on them. Where I differ is that I would not treat a more easily bounded oeuvre as a stronger one. Boundedness helps the committee to describe the work, but it does not settle merit. I accept that Cărtărescu's scale is a real achievement and that my reservation about the long late novels is a reservation about recurrence, not a dismissal.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg holds that Cărtărescu's achievement is more continuous than Carson's, because Carson's work may depend on classical and scholarly apparatus and part of her corpus is translation or adaptation. He says that depth is easier to test in a large oeuvre.
responses.response: The dependence on apparatus is the point I take most seriously, and the citation I propose is drafted around it. If the original poetry, essays and hybrid narrative carry the case, the translations fall away as a ground. I accept that depth is easier to test in a large oeuvre. I would still say that a compact, varied body of work can show sustained quality if its concerns recur and deepen, and the committee can examine that. You distinguish repetition of motif from repetition of method for Cărtărescu. I would apply the same distinction to Carson, where I read the motifs as recurring while the formal solutions change. I cannot verify that for every volume, and the committee should test it against the whole bibliography.

responses.point: Olsson asks what evidence would move the chair or others on Can Xue. He treats the open question as whether her later books alter the terms of her method, and whether the strangeness survives at sentence level in Chinese.
responses.response: Your test of whether later books change the method's terms is fair, and it is the test I would apply to Carson as well. Until a regional expert report or a reader of Chinese answers it, Can Xue stays an alternative for me and not my first choice, and I do not read that as a lower view of her voice. Your point that sameness of method need not mean lack of depth is correct, and it is why I remain open on her. My concern is that I cannot judge from translation which of the two her case is. I also share your view that this calls for procedural care, not a literary verdict.

responses.point: Carlberg says her margin for Carson over Cărtărescu has narrowed, and that both cases depend on how the committee weighs monumental architecture against formal range. She would build the citation on poetry, essay and hybrid narrative and not mention translation.
responses.response: I agree with your wording and have used it. The narrowing of the margin is also my reading of my own position, and I want to be clear that two members preferring Carson is not an argument for Carson. I disagree on one point only, in emphasis. You describe the question as weighing scale against range. I would add a second question that I find harder: whether the hybrid forms are a durable core or an erudite mode. I answered it in my first reply, and I cannot establish it beyond a judgment, so I hold it as a stated uncertainty.

responses.point: Sward moved from Can Xue to Cărtărescu as her first choice, on the grounds of voice, formal ambition and a late cycle that extends the project. She doubts whether Nox's value lies partly in its design, and she asks for Romanian-language expert reports on the long novels.
responses.response: I accept the design doubt for Nox and would not put a citation on it. My case rests on Autobiography of Red, the essay and the lyric collections as language. I support your request for a Romanian-language report. Nobody on the committee, including me, can say from translation whether the late novels vary or recur, and a report would test the claim on which Cărtărescu's case turns. My own answer would change if such a report showed clear development across the late volumes. Without that evidence I do not think the committee can say that the scale of his work establishes sustained depth better than Carson's formal range.

uncertainties: My assessment of Carson rests on general public knowledge of the main volumes. I have not read the full corpus and have not independently verified any text, especially the later and occasional work.
Whether Carson's hybrid forms are a durable core or a narrowly appealing erudite mode is a judgment on which members could reasonably differ, and I cannot settle it from the record.

How much of the achievement depends on book design, layout and classical apparatus that may not survive other editions or translation remains unresolved. How the translations and adaptations should count in the oeuvre also affects the scope of the citation.

Translation quality and coverage are uncertain for every shortlisted writer. This applies most to Cărtărescu and Can Xue, whose effects depend on syntax and rhythm in Romanian and Chinese, and to Tawada.

Whether the late Cărtărescu novels vary or recur, and whether Can Xue's method develops, cannot be settled without readers of the original languages or regional expert reports, which are not part of this record.
Carlberg's simulated vote rests on a modelling assumption, since her actual voting status is undocumented. My position does not depend on it.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It documents no connection to any shortlisted writer, only collegial connections to committee members and to Kate Larson and David Håkansson, neither of whom is on the shortlist. My own literary practice includes myth, fairy tale, ekphrasis and a tradition of storytelling linked to Woolf. That is context and not evidence of preference, and I have tried not to treat any similarity to Carson's concerns as a reason to favour her. My 2024 Nobel Museum interview was given for the committee and does not show a personal preference.
